newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower as growth concerns persist.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower as growth concerns persist.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended lower again on Tuesday as prices continued to adapt to the view that the economy grew briskly in the fourth quarter and with enough momentum to spur solid growth in early 1997.
"People realize that the fourth quarter was a good one for the economy," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
"Growth was not limited to the moderate, two-percent expansion that people were expecting at the start of the quarter," he said.
Many economists now estimate fourth-quarter growth at three percent or more, Moran said, and traders and investors are worried that that momentum will continue into 1997.
Moran said the government's data on November factory orders constituted more evidence of economic strength.

U.S. factory orders slipped 0.4 percent in November, the government reported, a smaller decline than economists had anticipated. The decline came after a revised 1.1 percent jump in factory orders in October.
Declines came in volatile areas like commercial aircraft, Moran said, areas that have been strong in prior months.
Meanwhile, there was a sizable, 0.8 percent rise in orders for non-durable goods.
"That implied that the manufacturing sector is doing well," said Moran.

Weekly reports on retail sales offset each other in terms of market impact, analysts said. The BTM Schroders report said U.S. adjusted chain store sales fell 1.0 percent in the week ended January 4 from the prior week. On the other hand, the Lynch, Jones & Ryan Redbook Retail Sales Index rose 0.7 percent in the five weeks of fiscal December versus November.

Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities Inc., said the market opened higher, taking its cue from overnight buying, "constructive comments" by Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Cathy Minehan on the economic outlook, and the weak BTM Schroders retail sales reading.

But several factors subsequently conspired to push the market into negative territory, including selling by a large hedge fund, sales by a foreign central bank, liquidation of long positions by a Middle Eastern account and heavy corporate debt issuance.
During the session, the 30-year bond yield climbed as high as 6.81 percent, its highest level since late October.
Some purchases of in the five-year sector and a little bit of short-covering cut the steepest of the session's losses in late trade.

"We may have moved as much as we're going to for the time being," said David Jones, vice chairman and chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "The signs of strengthening in economic activity as we closed 1996 and moved into early 1997 have been the dominant factor pushing yields higher. But we could be reaching an end to that process for now, at least."
The bellwether 30-year U.S. Treasury bond ended the day at 96-9/32, down 7/32, to yield 6.79 percent.
Three-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.02 percent. Six-month bill rates slipped one basis point to 5.09 percent. Year bill rates ended unchanged at 5.30 percent.

Two-year notes also ended unchanged at 99-19/32, yielding 5.97 percent. Five-year notes edged down 1/32 to 99-8/32, yielding 6.30 percent. Ten-year notes slipped 2/32 to 99-21/32, yielding 6.55 percent.
